repos.title: Matrix-Game 4.0: Harnessing Video Models for Real-Time Playable Game Worlds
repos.paper_summary:
Matrix-Game 4.0 is a real-time game-world system that separates game execution from visual generation. A lightweight engine keeps world state and enforces rules, a coding agent turns player requests into game code and captions, and an autoregressive video renderer turns low-poly proxy frames into detailed 480p frames.

The renderer adapts Wan2.2 5B to video-to-video generation. It is conditioned on the proxy, a per-frame caption built from engine state, reference frames, and the first frame. It is trained on 114,334 paired UE5 clips (1,712 hours), then distilled into a causal generator that produces four-frame chunks in one or two denoising steps.

On one RTX 5090 at 480p, the paper reports 60 FPS gameplay, 112 ms key-press-to-display latency, and 83 FPS single-step steady-state throughput with 18.2 GiB peak memory. Against the unoptimized causal baseline (4.5 FPS, 1110 ms), the cumulative optimizations give 19× throughput and 9.9× lower latency. The latency figure applies only to the evaluated configuration. The authors list lower inference cost, visual fidelity, higher-resolution refinement, and multiplayer rendering as future work.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Playable worlds need persistent state, executable rules and low latency, which motivates separating game logic from video generation.

digest_headlines.heading: Roadmap
digest_headlines.headline: A game engine, a coding agent and a video model form a harness, with the engine holding world state and enforcing rules.

digest_headlines.heading: Data
digest_headlines.headline: Paired Unreal Engine captures of low-poly and high-fidelity video give 114,334 training clips across four scene types.

digest_headlines.heading: Rendering Model
digest_headlines.headline: A video model is distilled into a causal generator that denoises each four-frame chunk in one or two steps.

digest_headlines.heading: Real-Time Inference
digest_headlines.headline: Cumulative optimizations raise steady-state throughput from 4.5 to 83.4 FPS and cut latency from 1110 ms to 112 ms.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: Visual results are qualitative only, but Matrix-Game 4.0 reports the lowest latency among four compared systems.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior interactive models keep dynamics in the network, while several recent systems assign rules to code and render with video.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion and Future Work
digest_headlines.headline: The harness design is offered as a reusable foundation, with lower inference cost and hardware needs left as near-term work.

repos.title: WeVisOne-VL: Unified Visual Perception from Objects to Pixels
repos.paper_summary: WeVisOne-VL is a vision-language model built on Qwen3-VL at 2B and 4B scales. It unifies object-level and pixel-level perception in one structured next-token output. Supported tasks include detection, referring localization, counting, OCR, referring segmentation, and image matting. Coordinates are emitted as dedicated tokens for values from 0 to 1000. After each predicted box, the model emits a special OBJ token. Its hidden state, the box, and multi-level ViT features feed a lightweight pixel decoder of about 9.6M parameters that predicts a mask or alpha matte. Training is three-stage SFT followed by GRPO-based mixed-task RL on samples where the SFT model is most uncertain. The data engine covers about 100M images and 3.6B box annotations, using detector proposals verified by a VLM and hard negatives for absent targets. The paper reports leading results across over 30 benchmarks, but the provided text gives no numeric scores. Stated limitations: limited general-purpose training data may reduce general capability, outputs are produced without chain-of-thought, and inference is single-turn.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Current vision-language models are unreliable for fine-grained perception, so this report proposes one model covering object-level and pixel-level tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: WeVisOne-VL Data Engine
digest_headlines.headline: The data engine yields over 100 million images and approximately 3.6 billion bounding-box annotations, with verification and error-driven refinement.

digest_headlines.heading: Model Design
digest_headlines.headline: The model writes tasks as text with coordinate tokens and adds a lightweight decoder that turns object tokens into full-resolution masks.

digest_headlines.heading: Training Pipeline
digest_headlines.headline: Training uses three supervised fine-tuning stages, then reinforcement learning on uncertainty-selected samples with box-based grounding rewards.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: WeVisOne-VL-4B reaches 57.1 mean F1 on COCO and 71.3 on Dense200, above the comparable VLMs listed.

digest_headlines.heading: Qualitative Analysis
digest_headlines.headline: Qualitative examples show finer instance separation, correct rejection of absent targets, and cleaner matte boundaries than the baselines.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work places the model among open-vocabulary detectors, grounded multimodal models, referring segmentation systems and promptable matting methods.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Limitations include possible loss of general capability, no chain-of-thought reasoning, single-turn prediction, and unclear user intent.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The model improves detection F1 and counting over comparable VLMs and surpasses the evaluated baselines on referring segmentation and matting.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists training corpus sources and counts, along with hyperparameters, pixel decoder training settings and RL reward definitions.

repos.title: OmniVoice: Towards Omnilingual Zero-Shot Text-to-Speech with Diffusion Language Models
repos.paper_summary:
OmniVoice is a zero-shot text-to-speech model covering over 600 languages. It is a single-stage non-autoregressive model: a bidirectional Transformer trained with a discrete masked diffusion objective maps text directly to 8-codebook acoustic tokens. Full-codebook random masking samples a mask for every token entry, so about 50% of tokens contribute to the loss, compared with one codebook per example in per-layer masking. The backbone is initialized from Qwen3-0.6B weights. The multilingual model trains on 581k hours from 50 open-source datasets.

On LibriSpeech-PC test-clean, it scores 0.729 SIM-o, 1.30 WER and 4.28 UTMOS, against 0.694, 1.59 and 4.28 for CosyVoice3. A bilingual variant trained on Emilia beats F5-TTS, ZipVoice and MaskGCT trained on the same corpus. Subjective SMOS is 3.80 versus 3.65 for Qwen3-TTS. On the 24-language MiniMax benchmark, Chinese character error rate is 1.008 versus 2.252 for MiniMax. Limitations: most baselines use different, larger training data; Cantonese word error rate is 17.709; and the FLEURS-102 results are not in the provided text.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing zero-shot speech models cover few languages, and two-stage discrete pipelines suffer error propagation and information bottlenecks.

digest_headlines.heading: Proposed Method
digest_headlines.headline: Full-codebook random masking and LLM initialization form the method, trained on more than 600 languages from 581k hours of audio.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Setup
digest_headlines.headline: Models are compared on Chinese, English and multilingual benchmarks using speaker similarity, error rates and subjective listening scores.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Results
digest_headlines.headline: OmniVoice gets the lowest word error rate on LibriSpeech-PC test-clean, at 1.30, and the highest subjective similarity score, at 3.80, among compared models.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusions
digest_headlines.headline: The authors conclude that the single-stage design, masking and LLM initialization together give broad language coverage and efficient inference.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists training datasets, inference-step and per-language results, supported languages, limitations and ethics statements.

repos.title: OmniEdu: Open Foundation Models for Learning and Teaching
repos.paper_summary: OmniEdu is an open family of K–12 educational foundation models (4B, 9B, and 27B, fine-tuned from Qwen3.5 and Qwen3.8 bases) trained on a corpus organized around four capabilities: subject competence, curriculum grounding, diagnostic reasoning, and pedagogical action and scaffolding. A six-stage pipeline cleans and decontaminates sources, audits and rewrites examples with an LLM, scores quality on 1–5 rubrics, and performs token-budgeted diversity selection with k-center greedy over BGE-M3 embeddings. Each example then receives one of 20 task-specific pedagogical system instructions. The final mixture has 69,999 examples (60,951 education-specific) and 15.96M supervised response tokens. Models are trained with LlamaFactory for 3 epochs and compared with base models, open educational LLMs, and proprietary models. OmniEdu-27B reaches 63.12% EM and 76.69% F1 on K12-Bench (base 52.11% EM), 85.89% on MathFish, 86.95% MaC on EDUMATH, 78.74% Scaffold win rate on MathTutorBench, and a 3.02 Teaching average on LongTutor. Limitations: the paper reports that EDUMATH MaC trails Kimi-K3 (90.00%), and the pipeline depends on proprietary LLM auditors and scorers.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Educational models need problem solving, curriculum structure, diagnosis, and teaching, but these are often built and tested separately.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work spans open educational models, data-selection methods, and benchmarks, while many frontier tutoring systems remain closed.

digest_headlines.heading: Data Preparation
digest_headlines.headline: A six-stage pipeline cleans, audits, scores, and selects 60,951 education examples, then adds general data and pedagogical instructions for 69,999 examples.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Tuning improves each base model at all three scales across curriculum, problem-solving, and tutoring benchmarks.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The conclusion argues capability-balanced supervision yields educational models that go beyond problem solving.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists per-subtask curriculum and general-capability tables and the full training configuration.

repos.title: FlexGlue: Sparse-to-Dense Feature Matching and Visual Disambiguation
repos.paper_summary: FlexGlue is a neural matcher that takes a set of query keypoints in one image and predicts their subpixel correspondences in the second image, while also predicting whether the pair is covisible so that non-overlapping pairs are rejected. A CNN backbone (frozen ConvNeXt-B with DINOv3 weights) produces a coarse token grid for each image. A 9-layer Transformer with self- and cross-attention updates the tokens, and a per-layer covisibility head can stop inference early on non-overlapping pairs. Each query gets a coarse position from a windowed softmax over cosine similarities, then a learned sub-cell offset. The model is trained on eight datasets with a joint correspondence, matchability, and covisibility loss. The paper reports that FlexGlue performs similarly to LoMa on sparse relative pose, is competitive with RoMav2 at lower cost, and gets the highest HardMatch mAA@10px in the sparse-to-dense setting. It also reports gains on ETH3D and IMC2025 SfM, InLoc, and a new indoor doppelganger benchmark built from LaMAR. Limitations include zero-shot evaluation on indoor disambiguation, since no indoor training data exists, and the paper notes that dense matching lacks robustness on HardMatch.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Sparse matchers are fast but detector-bound, dense matchers are costly, and both miss visual symmetries.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior matchers either inherit keypoint detector limits or add separate post-hoc disambiguation models; FlexGlue handles both in one network.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: FlexGlue aggregates context over dense token grids and reads out subpixel correspondences only at query keypoints, with covisibility heads.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Experiments show FlexGlue is competitive with dense matchers on relative pose at lower matching time, and it improves disambiguation, especially indoors.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The conclusion claims top accuracy on two multi-view reconstruction benchmarks and on disambiguation and localization benchmarks, at competitive cost.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists inference cost, keypoint detector results, benchmark curation, training details, matching modes, and limitations such as correlated errors and depth-edge accuracy drops.

repos.title: Raven: The Harness of Harnesses for Composable Agentic Intelligence
repos.paper_summary: Raven is an open-source multi-agent ecosystem that automatically constructs and orchestrates modular agent harnesses for long-horizon, cross-domain tasks. The Host Agent decomposes goals into subtasks, assigns them to specialized agents, and coordinates execution via a directed acyclic graph with explicit artifact dependencies. A diagnosis-driven evolution loop improves harness configurations by testing candidates against frozen task models, while Skill Forge retrieves reusable procedures from past executions. The paper establishes sufficient conditions under which composing multiple agents expands reliable task coverage beyond individual capabilities within a shared resource budget. On the new Multi-Agent Orchestration Benchmark (MAOB), Raven outperforms all baselines on four planning metrics using two backbone models, achieving Exact Match gains of 10.4 and 10.5 percentage points over the strongest competitor. Domain-specific evaluations show that native specialists perform competitively in research, coding, design, and operations. Experiments indicate that the curated skill library improves performance on three benchmarks, yielding larger gains than OpenClaw on two of them. The theoretical guarantees require specific compatibility conditions that may be difficult to verify for arbitrary third-party agents.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Raven composes model–harness agents through a host that plans, dispatches, and integrates work across domains.

digest_headlines.heading: Theory
digest_headlines.headline: Under a shared budget, sufficient conditions let composed agents reliably cover tasks that individual agents cannot reliably solve alone.

digest_headlines.heading: Multi-Agent Collaboration
digest_headlines.headline: A typed dependency graph is validated before dispatch, and every handoff passes through a recorded artifact.

digest_headlines.heading: Agent Harness Self-Evolution
digest_headlines.headline: Harness evolution edits a frozen model's strategy interfaces and keeps candidates only after paired screening.

digest_headlines.heading: Memory System
digest_headlines.headline: EverOS memory consolidates episodes into scenes and profiles, and Raven recalls them through hybrid retrieval.

digest_headlines.heading: Skill Forge
digest_headlines.headline: Skill Forge fuses skills from three sources, selects them through a gate, and revises skills from execution cases.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: Raven ranks first on all four graph metrics under both backbones, with Exact Match gains of 10.4 and 10.5 percentage points.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work spans orchestration, harness evolution, agent memory, and skills, which Raven combines with explicit boundaries.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion and Future Work
digest_headlines.headline: Raven's conclusion summarizes planning and skill results and proposes a multi-device network as future work.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix contains notation, execution semantics, the finite-query limit, and details of benchmark, grading, and ablation protocols.

repos.title: Skill Training with Corruption and Reconstruction Loop
repos.paper_summary: Skill Training with Corruption and Reconstruction Loop proposes a self-supervised way for LLM agents to learn domain skills as an external text library, without updating model weights, human annotations, or external rewards. Human-written short-drama screenplays are corrupted into story outlines, and the agent reconstructs each script using its skill library. A loss agent compares the reconstruction with the original and produces a textual loss report, and a backward agent edits the relevant skill cards. Skill cards are routed into Mixture-of-Experts folders, and a linter caps each card at 1,200 tokens to limit memorization. Training uses 20 novels with three epochs and Claude Sonnet 4.6. Evaluation holds out six novels (385 episodes) and compares four configurations: Base (empty library), +Few-shot, +Distill, and +Ours. The paper reports ten event-based metrics designed with professionals, and the abstract states that generation quality improves on unseen stories. The main limitations are that the training corpus is proprietary and that the evaluation is limited to short-drama screenwriting.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Fine-tuning large language models is costly and opaque, and hand-written skills are a bottleneck, motivating self-supervised skill acquisition.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior skill methods need costly human writing or successful trajectories, so the authors summarize and reconstruct high-quality examples instead.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: A corruption-and-reconstruction loop trains a skill library, with capacity limits and micro-step updates to keep it organized.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Held-out evaluation compares four configurations across 385 episodes from six unseen stories using ten metrics.

repos.title: LightRAG: Simple and Fast Retrieval-Augmented Generation
repos.paper_summary:
LightRAG is a graph-based retrieval-augmented generation system. An LLM extracts entities and relations from chunks of size 1200, profiles each as a key-value pair, and deduplicates the resulting graph. At query time, local keywords match entities and global keywords match relations, and one-hop neighbors of the matches are added as context for a general LLM. New documents are indexed by merging their subgraphs into the existing graph instead of rebuilding it.

The evaluation uses four UltraDomain datasets (Agriculture, CS, Legal, Mix), with 125 generated questions per dataset, GPT-4o-mini as the default LLM, and pairwise LLM judgments reported as win rates. Against NaiveRAG on Legal, LightRAG wins 84.8% overall. Against GraphRAG, the margins are small: overall win rates of 54.8% on Agriculture, 52.0% on CS, 52.8% on Legal, and 49.6% on Mix.

The judgments come from a single LLM judge, not human or ground-truth labels. The ablation and cost results are cut off in the provided text, so this summary does not report them.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing RAG systems rely on flat representations and produce fragmented answers, so the paper proposes graph-based indexing with incremental updates.

digest_headlines.heading: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
digest_headlines.headline: The paper formalizes RAG as indexing and retrieval followed by generation, and sets three design goals for an efficient system.

digest_headlines.heading: The LightRAG Architecture
digest_headlines.headline: LightRAG builds a knowledge graph with LLM extraction, updates it incrementally, and retrieves through dual-level keyword matching.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: LightRAG wins LLM-judged comparisons against four baselines on UltraDomain datasets, and uses far fewer retrieval tokens than GraphRAG.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work finds graph-based RAG lacks dynamic updates, and surveys three ways LLMs are combined with graph data.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: LightRAG is concluded to improve retrieval speed and quality and cut LLM inference costs through graph indexing and incremental updates.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists dataset statistics, a case study against NaiveRAG, and the prompts for graph generation, query generation, keyword extraction and evaluation.

repos.title: SUPRA-TEX: 3D Generation with Super-Aligned Texture
repos.paper_summary: SUPRA-Tex generates relightable 3D assets with PBR materials from a single reference image, keeping the reference's text, logos, and patterns at their visible surface locations. A 2D model built on a multimodal DiT predicts albedo and metallic-roughness maps in the reference view in one forward pass, taking 1.2 s on one H800. These maps are projected onto visible surface voxels and encoded by the frozen pretrained material VAE encoder into observation latents, which carry coverage and boundary-distance metadata. An interleaved flow transformer then generates full-surface material latents with flow matching. Observation latents serve as fixed, read-only memory, and blocks alternate between updating unobserved cells and the full surface. The 2D estimator is trained on Objaverse renders. The paper reports the best results among the evaluated methods in geometry-conditioned texturing and end-to-end generation, but the provided Table 1 excerpt cuts off before the SUPRA-Tex row, so this summary gives no SUPRA-Tex scores. Stated limitations include errors from upstream geometry or 2D material estimation, inconsistent completion across visibility boundaries, and qualitative-only failure cases with no paired two-view result.

digest_headlines.heading: 1 Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Multi-view fusion and native 3D generation both lose fine reference details, motivating a split into material estimation, alignment and completion.

digest_headlines.heading: 2 Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior texturing either fuses inconsistent multi-view predictions or conditions a native generator on implicit image features.

digest_headlines.heading: 3 Method
digest_headlines.headline: SUPRA-Tex estimates reference-view PBR maps, encodes them as fixed observation anchors, and completes the full-surface material latents.

digest_headlines.heading: 4 Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: SUPRA-Tex leads all shaded and PBR metrics in given-geometry texturing on both evaluation datasets.

digest_headlines.heading: 5 Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Errors in upstream geometry, 2D material estimates and unobserved regions limit fidelity and asset quality.

digest_headlines.heading: 6 Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Trained only on public data, SUPRA-Tex reaches top results among evaluated methods and is competitive with commercial systems.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix gives training data, optimization, evaluation protocols, ablations, extra qualitative comparisons and a notation table.

repos.title: Democratizing Robot-Use Agents: A Unified Harness with Open Models
repos.paper_summary: uni-robot-agent is a unified, modular harness that lets open-weight models act as robot-use agents in simulation and on physical robots. It gives agents shared tools with common units and feedback across environments through per-environment adapters, overlaps model reasoning with tool execution, and binds images, calibration, and robot state to immutable snapshots. On RoboDojo's 42 simulation tasks (252 episodes), Qwen3.8-Flash-Next with the harness scores 31.39 with 25.00% success. This is above the published GPT-6 Astra–RoboProbe result of 28.97 and the listed VLA and WAM baselines, and the agent receives no simulator depth or task-verifier feedback. On 19 real-world tabletop tasks it scores 49.50, above Dream-1 (35.50) and close to a fine-tuned $\pi_{0.5}$ (47.75). Limitations: real-world agents receive RealSense depth while $\pi_{0.5}$ and Dream-1 use RGB only; precise manipulation and long-horizon execution remain weak, and Qwen and DeepSeek trail Xiaomi-Robotics-1 and OpenWAM-$\alpha$ on long-horizon tasks. Trajectory analysis finds four failure patterns, which the authors link to visual understanding, spatial grounding, geometric coding, and embodied reasoning.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Proprietary models block robot-use training, so this paper offers an open, trainable harness that reaches competitive scores.

digest_headlines.heading: uni-robot-agent: A Unified and Modular Harness
digest_headlines.headline: Shared tools, five logical layers, and six design choices let agents run without simulator depth or verifier feedback.

digest_headlines.heading: Can Open Models Use Robots in Simulation and the Real World?
digest_headlines.headline: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next reaches 31.39 Score on RoboDojo and 49.50 on 19 real-world tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: What Capabilities Enable Robot-Use Agents?
digest_headlines.headline: Robot use appears across model generations and families, and four failure types suggest joint training targets.

digest_headlines.heading: Analysis on Privileged Information
digest_headlines.headline: Removing camera parameters drops Qwen to 9.13, while removing skills changes Score from 31.39 to 30.31.

digest_headlines.heading: Analysis on Cost and Speed
digest_headlines.headline: Qwen costs 1.09 USD per episode for 31.39 Score, and pipelining cuts episode time on all five tested tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior robot-use harnesses offer varied tools and interfaces, so this work separates shared tools from model runtimes.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: An open-weight model with the harness reaches 31.39 Score, while precise manipulation and long-horizon execution remain open.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists baselines, real-world task catalogue and scoring rules, per-task results, and agent case studies.
